# The Retiring of Words

Every autumn, the town of Hesk retires a word.

Nobody remembers exactly how it started. My grandmother says it was a drought year, and the council, having nothing useful to do about the rain, decided to do something about language instead. Others say it was a widower who petitioned to have his wife's name struck from common use so he wouldn't hear it shouted across the market at some other Margaret. Whatever the origin, it stuck. Each October we gather in the grain hall, nominations are read aloud, and by show of hands one word is put out to pasture.

After that, you don't say it. Not as punishment. There's no fine and no jail. It's more like how you don't wear shoes in someone's kitchen once you've been told. You just stop.

The retired words are painted on the long beam above the hall's doors, white on black, so we don't forget what we've given up. *Hurry* is up there, from the year before I was born. *Deadline*. *Whatever*, which caused a real scandal among the teenagers. *Fine*, which my mother says was the hardest; for months people stood in doorways with their mouths open, unable to answer *how are you* without it, forced to say something true instead.

That's the thing nobody tells visitors. Retiring a word doesn't remove the feeling behind it. It just takes away the shortcut. When you can't say *hurry*, you have to say *I'm frightened we'll miss the train* or *I want to be home with you already*. The feeling has to walk the long way around, and it arrives changed.

---

This year my grandmother nominated *later*.

She stood up slowly, one hand on the back of Mr. Aldane's chair, and said it plainly. There was a murmur. *Later* is a working word. Farmers use it, and shopkeepers, and parents. *Later* is how the whole town gets through a day.

"Reasons?" asked the clerk, as is the custom.

My grandmother looked around the hall. She's eighty-one and has buried a husband and a son and more friends than she will count aloud. She has a way of looking at a room as if she's already fond of it and slightly disappointed.

"Because I've been saying it my whole life," she said, "and I'd like to know what happens if I can't."

She sat down. That was all.

---

The other nominations that year were *actually*, which the schoolteacher proposed with great feeling, and *literally*, which was mostly a joke. *Busy* had some support. Someone in the back nominated *sorry*, and there was a short, heated debate about whether it was a word people overused or a word people didn't use enough, which is the kind of argument Hesk loves best.

Then the hands went up.

I watched my grandmother while they counted. She didn't raise her own hand for *later*. She said afterward it felt like voting for yourself in a school election. But she watched the room with her lips pressed tight, and when the clerk announced it, forty-one to twenty-six, she let out a breath I don't think she knew she'd been holding.

The painter was already on his ladder by the time we filed out.

---

The first week was ridiculous. You don't realize how often you defer until you can't. At the bakery, Mrs. Tolliver started to tell a customer she'd have the rye ready *la—* and stopped, flustered, and finally said, "At four o'clock. I'll have it at four." Which was more useful anyway.

Children were the worst off. *Can we go to the river? Later.* *Will you read to me? Later.* *Can I tell you something? Later, love, I'm cooking.* Without the word, parents had to choose. Yes or no. Now or a specific time they would be held to. I heard a man on Cooper Street tell his daughter, "I'm too tired right now, and I'm sorry, and tomorrow after supper I promise," and the girl just nodded, satisfied, because a promise with edges is easier to carry than a fog.

The second week, things got quieter and stranger.

People started doing things. Not all of them, and not all at once. But the fence at the Brennan place, which had been leaning since spring, got fixed. Old Harold Pym, who'd been meaning to write to his brother in the city for eleven years, walked into the post office with a letter so thick they had to charge him double. The schoolteacher, who had lost the vote for *actually*, finally took the painting course she'd talked about since I was her student.

It wasn't that *later* had been stopping anyone. It was that *later* had been a soft place to set things down, and now there was no soft place. You either held the thing or you dropped it. And it turns out when people have to look at what they're dropping, they drop less.

---

I asked my grandmother, near the end of that month, what she'd found out.

We were on her porch. The light was going the color it goes in Hesk in late October, like weak tea. She had a blanket over her knees and was shelling beans she had no real need to shell.

"About what?"

"About what happens when you can't say it."

She thought for a while. A long while. Long enough that I would once have said *tell me later* and gone inside.

"I found out I'd been lying," she said finally. "Not badly. The ordinary way. I'd say *later* and mean *never*, or *I'm scared*, or *I don't think I deserve that yet*." She split a pod with her thumbnail. "Your grandfather wanted to go to the coast. The whole last year. I kept saying later."

I didn't say anything. There wasn't a word for it that hadn't been retired.

"So," she said, brushing her hands off on her apron. "I bought two train tickets this morning. You're coming with me. Thursday."

"Thursday," I said.

"Thursday," she said, and put the beans aside, and looked out over the town as if she were already fond of it, and for once not disappointed at all.
